rationales: Most enzymes are not nucleic acids, although a few catalytic RNA molecules exist.
Most enzymes are proteins, making this the best answer.
Carbohydrates are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Lipids are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Some enzymes break down food, but that does not define all enzymes.
Enzymes are not hormones, even though some hormones affect metabolism.
An enzyme is generally a protein that speeds up chemical reactions without being consumed.
Energy storage is not the defining function of an enzyme.
Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme may lose activity rather than continuing to speed up.
High temperatures can alter an enzyme’s shape, including its active site, and reduce its activity.
An enzyme does not necessarily remain stable at temperatures above its optimum.
An enzyme catalyzes reactions and is not converted into a substrate.
An enzyme’s active site has a shape and chemical properties suited to particular substrates, giving it specificity.
Being a protein alone does not explain why an enzyme acts on specific substrates.
Enzymes are generally not consumed in the reactions they catalyze.
Enzymes do not work only at high temperatures; each has conditions under which it works best.
Not all enzymes require prosthetic groups to function.
Prosthetic groups are non-protein components, not proteins.
A prosthetic group is tightly bound rather than loosely attached to its enzyme.
Prosthetic groups are tightly bound non-protein components of enzymes.
Increasing temperature generally increases enzyme activity up to an optimum, after which activity can decline.
Temperature does not always decrease activity; moderate increases can speed enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
An enzyme does not become non-functional with every increase in temperature.
Temperature affects enzyme activity by changing reaction rates and, at high levels, enzyme structure.
A competitive inhibitor, rather than the substrate, binds to the enzyme’s active site.
Changing the enzyme’s shape is characteristic of some noncompetitive or allosteric inhibition, not competitive inhibition.
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and prevents substrate binding.
Competitive inhibitors do not characteristically block cofactors.
A pH far below the enzyme’s optimum can alter the active site and reduce substrate binding.
An acidic solution does not necessarily make the enzyme work faster; pH 4.0 is far from its stated optimum.
Acidity does not cause an enzyme to gain additional active sites.
The question describes an effect on the enzyme, and substrates are not universally rendered inactive by acidic conditions.
In the induced fit model, substrate binding induces a shape change in the enzyme’s active site.
The model primarily describes a change in the enzyme’s shape, not the substrate changing shape to fit.
The induced fit model involves a shape change in the active site.
The substrate binds at the active site in the induced fit model, not at a different site.
Pepsin functions best in the acidic stomach, while trypsin functions best in the more alkaline small intestine.
Pepsin does not work best at high pH, so both enzymes do not work best at high pH.
Trypsin does not work best at low pH, so both enzymes do not work best at low pH.
This reverses their usual optima: pepsin works at low pH and trypsin at higher pH.
